Measure re-identification risk from quasi-identifiers

Source: R/anon_risk.R
anon_risk.Rd

Measures how easily subjects could be singled out from the combination of their quasi-identifiers (indirect identifiers such as age, sex, race, ethnicity, site, height or weight). Each subject's group is the set of subjects with exactly the same quasi-identifier values; k is the group's size and the subject's risk is 1 / k. Quasi-identifiers can come from several datasets linked by key.

Usage

anon_risk(data, quasi, key = "USUBJID", max_risk = 0.09)

Arguments

data

A data frame, a named list of data frames linked by key, or the result of a de-identification step such as anon_subject_ids().

quasi

The quasi-identifiers to measure. For a single data frame, a character vector of column names. For a list of data frames, a list whose named elements are character vectors of columns in the dataset of that name (each subject must have one value per column, as in dm), and whose unnamed elements are anon_quasi_values() specifications for values that vary by row, such as baseline height and weight in vs.

key

Name of the subject identifier column shared by the datasets. It must have the same type (character or factor, or numeric) in every dataset used.

max_risk

Highest acceptable re-identification risk for any subject (the maximum risk, 1 / k for the smallest group). The target group size is the smallest k with 1 / k <= max_risk, allowing for floating-point error so that 0.1 and 1/3 give 10 and 3. The default, 0.09, is the threshold Health Canada and EMA encourage for public release of clinical information, and requires groups of at least 12. Health Canada equates 0.09 with a cell size of 11, but 1 / 11 is about 0.0909; to use groups of 11, pass max_risk = 1/11. See Details.

Value

An object of class "anon_risk", a list with:

  • summary: one row with n_subjects, n_quasi, max_risk_target (the max_risk argument), k_target (the group size it requires), n_unique (subjects in a group of one), min_k, max_risk (the observed maximum, 1 / min_k), avg_risk (mean of 1 / k over subjects, equal to the number of groups divided by n_subjects), n_below_k (subjects in groups smaller than k_target), prop_below_k and meets_target (min_k >= k_target).

  • drivers: one row per quasi-identifier with the number of distinct non-missing values (n_values), the number of missing values (n_missing), and n_unique_without, n_below_k_without, min_k_without and avg_risk_without (the result if that variable were left out). Rows are ordered so the variable whose removal helps most comes first: by n_below_k_without, then n_unique_without, then avg_risk_without (all ascending), then the order of quasi.

  • quasi, key: the quasi-identifier names and key used.

  • sources: one row per quasi-identifier giving where it comes from: variable, dataset, and either column or test_col, test and result_col, plus filtered (whether a filter was used). The filter itself is not stored, because it may contain identifying values.

The object holds counts only, no subject-level rows or key values. Use anon_risk_subjects() for per-subject results.

Details

Subjects are all non-missing key values found in the datasets used by quasi; rows with a missing or blank key are dropped with a warning, and a warning is given if keys differ only by leading or trailing spaces. A subject with no value for a quasi-identifier (for example, missing from vs) gets NA for it, and NA is treated as a value of its own when forming groups. Blank strings, which is how SAS transport (XPT) files store missing text, are treated as missing. Values are otherwise grouped by exact equality.

Risk is measured on one value per subject for each quasi-identifier. A copy shared with others usually contains every row of a dataset (for example weight at every visit), and any row can identify a subject as well as the measured one. The measurement only describes a shared copy if every row of each quasi-identifier is generalized or removed in the same way.

Risk is measured against the subjects in data only. Health Canada and EMA allow or encourage measuring risk against a larger reference population, which gives lower risk; measuring within the data, the smallest population, is the strictest reading.

The default target comes from Health Canada's Public Release of Clinical Information guidance. Its "Risk Threshold" section "encourages adopting a 9% re-identification risk threshold (risk=0.09)", and its section on measuring risk states "Adopting a risk threshold of risk=0.09 equates to a target cell size of 11 patients" (https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drug-health-product-review-approval/profile-public-release-clinical-information-guidance/document.html). EMA's Anonymisation Report Form Instructions (EMA/482639/2023) state that "Health Canada PRCI and EMA Policy 0070 guidance encourages a 9% re-identification risk threshold (risk=0.09)" and describe the target as a maximum "that should not be exceeded" (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/other/anonymisation-report-form-instructions_en.pdf). Because 1 / 11 (about 0.0909) exceeds 0.09, the default requires groups of at least 12 so that the threshold is never exceeded; max_risk = 1/11 follows Health Canada's stated cell size instead. Both set the threshold for public release of clinical documents; using it for other sharing is a deliberately conservative choice. GDPR and HIPAA set no numerical re-identification risk threshold. Meeting the target is evidence about re-identification risk from the chosen quasi-identifiers, not proof that data is anonymous or de-identified under any regime.

The drivers table shows what leaving out each quasi-identifier on its own would achieve. It cannot see variables that identify the same subjects together (for example height and weight), it shows the effect of removing a variable rather than generalizing it, and it does not measure information loss. Use it to decide what to try next, then measure again.

See also

anon_risk_subjects() for per-subject group sizes.

Examples

dm <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = sprintf("S%02d", 1:6),
  AGE = c(60, 60, 60, 70, 70, 85),
  SEX = c("F", "F", "F", "M", "M", "M")
)
anon_risk(dm, quasi = c("AGE", "SEX"), max_risk = 1/3)
#> Re-identification risk
#> ======================
#> 
#> Quasi-identifiers: AGE, SEX 
#> Subjects: 6 
#> Target: maximum risk 0.3333333 (groups of at least 3) 
#> Maximum risk: 1 (smallest group: 1)  Average risk: 0.5 
#> Unique subjects (group of 1): 1 
#> Subjects in groups smaller than 3: 3 (50%)
#> Meets target: no 
#> 
#> Drivers (`_without` columns: result if that variable alone were left out):
#>  variable n_values n_missing n_unique_without n_below_k_without min_k_without
#>       AGE        3         0                0                 0             3
#>       SEX        2         0                1                 3             1
#>  avg_risk_without
#>         0.3333333
#>         0.5000000

vs <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = rep(dm$USUBJID, each = 2),
  VSTESTCD = rep(c("HEIGHT", "WEIGHT"), 6),
  VSSTRESN = c(160, 60, 160, 60, 165, 62, 180, 80, 180, 80, 175, 90),
  VSBLFL = "Y"
)
# Dropping any single variable changes nothing here: subjects 1-2 and 4-5
# match on every variable, and HEIGHT and WEIGHT single out the same
# subjects, which leave-one-out drivers cannot show.
anon_risk(
  list(dm = dm, vs = vs),
  quasi = list(
    dm = c("AGE", "SEX"),
    anon_quasi_values("vs", "VSTESTCD", c("HEIGHT", "WEIGHT"), "VSSTRESN",
                      filter = ~ VSBLFL == "Y")
  ),
  max_risk = 0.5
)
#> Re-identification risk
#> ======================
#> 
#> Quasi-identifiers: AGE, SEX, HEIGHT, WEIGHT 
#> Subjects: 6 
#> Target: maximum risk 0.5 (groups of at least 2) 
#> Maximum risk: 1 (smallest group: 1)  Average risk: 0.6666667 
#> Unique subjects (group of 1): 2 
#> Subjects in groups smaller than 2: 2 (33.3%)
#> Meets target: no 
#> 
#> Drivers (`_without` columns: result if that variable alone were left out):
#>  variable n_values n_missing n_unique_without n_below_k_without min_k_without
#>       AGE        3         0                2                 2             1
#>       SEX        2         0                2                 2             1
#>    HEIGHT        4         0                2                 2             1
#>    WEIGHT        4         0                2                 2             1
#>  avg_risk_without
#>         0.6666667
#>         0.6666667
#>         0.6666667
#>         0.6666667
